title: STATE OF SOUTH CAROLINA (01-ALJ-19-0152-CC)
text:
STATE OF SOUTH CAROLINA
ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGE DIVISION
Willie A. Key, ) Docket No. 01-ALJ-19-0152-CC
)
Petitioner, )
)
v. ) FINAL ORDER
) AND DECISION
South Carolina Department of )
Transportation, )
)
Respondent. )
)
APPEARANCES: Willie A. Key, pro se
Deborah B. Durden, Esquire, for the Respondent
STATEMENT OF THE CASE
This matter is before the Administrative Law Judge Division (“Division”) pursuant to the
request of the Petitioner, Willie A. Key, for a contested case hearing pursuant to S.C. Code Ann.
§28-11-10, et seq. (Supp. 2000), S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 63-322 (Supp. 2000), and 24 C.F.R. § 24.1 et
seq. Petitioner seeks review of a decision of the Respondent, South Carolina Department of
Transportation (“Department”), awarding the Petitioner relocation assistance benefits. After notice
to the parties, a contested case hearing was held on June 5, 2001, at the offices of the Division in
Columbia, South Carolina.
For the following reasons, I find that the Department’s decision to award the Petitioner Ten
Thousand Five Hundred Dollars ($10,500) in relocation assistance benefits was proper.
FINDINGS OF FACT
After consideration and review of all the evidence and testimony and having judged the
credibility of the witnesses, by a preponderance of the evidence, I make the following findings of
fact:

1. Notice of the date, time, place and subject matter of the hearing was timely given to
the parties.
2. The Petitioner is the tenant of an apartment located at 18-B Boyer Court, Charleston,
South Carolina. The apartment building in which Petitioner resides is being acquired by the
Department in conjunction with the construction of the new Cooper River bridge.
3. 18-B Boyer Court is located in a mixed industrial/commercial and residential area in
the upper peninsula of Charleston. The building backs up to Interstate 26, which is an elevated
multi-lane highway, and is located in a predominantly minority neighborhood on a dead end street.
The apartment building is constructed of concrete blocks and is two stories high. See Respondent’s
Exhibit 7.
4. Petitioner’s apartment is located on the ground floor of the building. It consists of a
living room, a kitchen/dining room, two bedrooms and one bath. The walls of the apartment are
paneled and the floors are vinyl tile. The apartment has electric heat as well as window units for air
conditioning. Petitioner pays $350.00 per month in rent. He had occupied the apartment for more
than 90 days prior to the Department’s offer of relocation assistance benefits.
5. Petitioner is employed as a supervisor by AVM Janitorial Service in Mt. Pleasant,
South Carolina. He was formerly employed as a paralegal and at a Dollar General store. Petitioner
owns his own vehicle and presently uses it to travel to his employment in Mt. Pleasant.
6. In order to compute the amount of relocation assistance benefits Petitioner was
entitled to as a result of the Department’s acquisition of his apartment building, the Department’s
relocation agent, Ms. Claudia Wilkes, inspected the Petitioner’s apartment, filled out an inspection
report listing the features of the apartment, and performed a study of comparable rental housing in
the Charleston peninsula area. Comparables in the Charleston peninsula area were studied because
the Petitioner’s present apartment is located in that area. As is the Department’s standard procedure
in such matters, Ms. Wilkes selected three comparable rental dwellings and computed the amount of
benefits based upon the rent for the dwelling which was deemed most comparable to Petitioner’s
apartment.
7. The first comparable property, 443 Hanover Street, is located approximately three
blocks from Petitioner’s apartment. The property is in a similar neighborhood to Petitioner’s
2

neighborhood, but it is located farther from Interstate 26. This property is a two bedroom, one bath
single family dwelling which is constructed of concrete blocks. It rents for $600.00 per month. See
Respondent’s Exhibit 8.
8. The second comparable property is at 900 Rutledge Avenue. It is located on the
upper peninsula of Charleston and is several blocks away from Interstate 26. This property is a two
bedroom, one bath apartment which is located on the ground floor of a single family dwelling which
has been converted into three apartments. It rents for $600.00 per month. The property is in a better
neighborhood than Petitioner’s present neighborhood, because it is farther from major highways and
is in an entirely residential area with paved streets and sidewalks. See Respondent’s Exhibits 5 and
9. The neighborhood is a racially mixed neighborhood. The landlord, who is white, lives on the
premises. The apartment has wall-to-wall carpeting and central heating and air conditioning, and is
very well kept. It is a more desirable unit than Petitioner’s current apartment. The Department
determined that this unit was the most comparable to Petitioner’s current apartment, and computed
Petitioner’s relocation assistance benefits based on the $600.00 per month rent for this apartment.
9. The third comparable property is at 305 Grove Street. It is a two bedroom, one and
one-half bath townhouse style apartment located in the Hampton Park area near The Citadel. This
apartment has hardwood floors, large rooms, and central heating and air conditioning. It is a more
desirable unit than Petitioner’s current apartment. The neighborhood is racially diverse and is
entirely residential with paved streets and sidewalks. It is located some distance from major
thoroughfares and is a more desirable neighborhood than Petitioner’s present neighborhood. 305
Grove Street rents for $800.00 per month. See Respondent’s Exhibits 5 and 10.
10. The Department’s determination that 900 Rutledge Avenue was most comparable to
Petitioner’s present apartment was based on Ms. Wilkes’ inspection of both apartments, a
comparison of the features of each apartment, and the location of both apartments. See Respondent’s
Exhibit 5.
11. On November 9, 2000, the Department made an offer of relocation assistance benefits
to the Petitioner. The offer consisted of $1,075 for moving expenses and $10,500 in rental
assistance. The $10,500 was computed based upon a monthly payment of $250.00 (the difference
between the Petitioner’s present rent of $350.00 per month and the rent for 900 Rutledge Avenue,
3

the apartment identified as most comparable, at $600.00 per month), for 42 months, the maximum
time allowed by law. The offer of $10,500 is contingent upon the Petitioner actually renting an
apartment for at least $600.00 per month. If Petitioner rents an apartment with lower monthly rent,
the amount of benefits would be recomputed accordingly. The $1,075 for moving expenses is not at
issue in this case.
12. During the time that Ms. Wilkes was attempting to assist the Petitioner in finding
comparable rental housing, she would deliver lists of available rental units to the Petitioner’s home
from time to time. See Respondent’s Exhibit 11. The Petitioner never asked to see any of the
comparables nor any of the other units Ms. Wilkes identified. Instead, he indicated to Ms. Wilkes
that he was interested in moving to another area, such as the Myrtle Beach area, Buies Creek, North
Carolina, or Falls Church, Virginia. He did not ask Ms. Wilkes to research apartments in the Mt.
Pleasant area. Ms. Wilkes informed the Petitioner that, although he could live anywhere he wanted
to, the amount of relocation assistance benefits had to be based on the cost of comparable housing in
the Charleston peninsula area.
13. Petitioner rejected the Department’s offer of $10,500 as being too low.
Thereafter, he filed a request for a contested case hearing before the Division. He requests
benefits computed on a rent of at least $725 per month, which he states is necessary in order
for him to rent a comparable apartment in Mt. Pleasant near his place of employment.
14. Petitioner presented several examples of apartments in Mt. Pleasant which he states
should be used as comparable rental units for the computation of benefits. Petitioner identified River
Oaks Apartments, Runaway Bay Apartments, and Daniel’s Landing as comparable to his present
apartment. A two bedroom apartment at River Oaks rents for a minimum of $825.00 per month; at
Runaway Bay, for a minimum of $799.00 per month; and at Daniel’s Landing, for a minimum of
$925.00 per month. See Respondent’s Exhibit 12. All of these apartments are luxury apartments
located in new or relatively new apartment complexes, with amenities such as swimming pools,
screened porches, fireplaces, clubhouses, and tennis courts. Id. at pages 29, 47, and 50. These
complexes are located in far more desirable areas and have many more amenities than Petitioner’s
present apartment.
4

CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
Based upon the foregoing Findings of Fact, I conclude, as a matter of law, the following:
1. This Division has personal and subject matter jurisdiction.
2. Pursuant to S.C. Code Ann. § 28-11-10 (Rev. 1991), the Department is required to
make relocation assistance payments to persons displaced when the Department acquires property
through the power of eminent domain, subject to the provisions of 49 C.F.R. Part 24.
3. Pursuant to S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 63-322 (Supp. 2000), a person aggrieved by a
decision of the Department regarding relocation assistance payments may seek relief by requesting a
contested case hearing before the Division.
4. 49 C.F.R. Part 24 contains the criteria which the Department must follow in
determining a person’s entitlement to relocation assistance payments. 49 C.F.R. § 24.402 (a)(1)
provides, as a general rule, that a tenant displaced from a dwelling is entitled to a payment not to
exceed $5,250.00 for rental assistance if that person had actually and lawfully occupied the
displacement dwelling for at least 90 days immediately prior to the initiation of negotiations for the
purchase of the dwelling by the Department. In this case, Petitioner met the 90-day occupancy
requirement.
5. Rental assistance payments are generally computed by subtracting the base monthly
rental for the displacement dwelling from the monthly rent and estimated average monthly cost of
utilities for a comparable replacement dwelling, and multiplying that amount by 42. See 49 C.F.R. §
24.402 (b). In most instances, the maximum rental assistance payment may not exceed $5,250.00.
Id. However, an exception to the general rule exists in situations where comparable replacement
dwellings are not available within the monetary limits specified in § 24.402 (b). In such an instance,
the Department is authorized to make a determination, either on a case-by-case basis or for a project
as a whole, that “last resort” housing assistance is justified. See 49 C.F.R. § 24.404 (a). If such
assistance is justified, the Department may provide a replacement housing payment in excess of the
standard monetary limit of $5,250.00, either in installments or in a lump sum. 49 C.F.R. § 24.404
(c)(1)(i). The Department made a determination that last resort housing assistance was justified for
the entire Cooper River bridge project because of the scarcity of available comparable replacement
housing in the Charleston peninsula area. For this reason, the Department offered Petitioner a rental
5

assistance payment in the lump sum of $10,500.00, an amount significantly greater than the normal
limit of $5,250. This sum was computed by subtracting the monthly rent for Petitioner’s present
apartment from the monthly rent for the comparable unit at 900 Rutledge Avenue and then
multiplying that amount by 42. See Finding of Fact 11.
6. The Petitioner argues that the $10,500 rental assistance payment is too low and that
the Department should have computed his rental assistance payment on the basis of the rental cost of
apartments in Mt. Pleasant, where he is employed. Petitioner estimates that cost at a minimum of
$725.00 per month. However, regardless of whether a replacement housing payment is made under
the provisions of 49 C.F.R. § 24.402 or the “last resort” provisions of 49 C.F.R. § 24.404, the upper
limit of a replacement housing payment must be based upon the cost of a comparable replacement
dwelling. See 49 C.F.R. § 24.403 (a). The Department is required to examine at least three
comparable replacement dwellings, if available, and to compute the payment on the basis of the
dwelling most nearly representative of, and equal to or better than the displacement dwelling. Id. at
§ 24.403(a)(1). Furthermore, to the extent feasible, comparable replacement dwellings “shall be
selected from the neighborhood in which the displacement dwelling was located or, if this is not
possible, in nearby or similar neighborhoods where housing costs are generally the same or higher.”
Id. at § 24.403 (a)(4). In this case, the Department examined three comparable replacement
dwellings in the upper Charleston peninsula area, the area in which the Petitioner’s present apartment
is located, and computed the rental assistance payment on the basis of the monthly rent for 900
Rutledge Avenue, the dwelling which was deemed most comparable to the Petitioner’s present
apartment.
7. 49 C.F.R. § 24.2 defines a “comparable replacement dwelling” as follows:
The term “comparable replacement dwelling” means a dwelling which is:
(1) Decent, safe, and sanitary as described in paragraph (f) of this section;
(2) Functionally equivalent to the displacement dwelling. The term “functionally
equivalent” means that it performs the same function, provides the same utility, and
is capable of contributing to a comparable style of living. While a comparable
replacement dwelling need not possess every feature of the displacement dwelling,
the principal features must be present. . . .
(3) Adequate in size to accommodate the occupants;
(4) In an area not subject to unreasonable adverse environmental conditions;
6

(5) In a location generally not less desirable than the location of the displaced
person’s dwelling with respect to public utilities and commercial and public facilities,
and reasonably accessible to the person’s place of employment;
(6) On a site that is typical in size for residential development with normal site
improvements. . . .
(7) Currently available to the displaced person on the private market. . . . and
(8) Within the financial means of the displaced person.
I conclude that 900 Rutledge Avenue is a “comparable replacement dwelling” as defined above.
Although Petitioner claims that this dwelling is located in a predominantly minority, high crime
neighborhood, the regulations require only that the comparable replacement dwelling be located in a
neighborhood not less desirable than the location of the displacement dwelling. There is no evidence
that the neighborhood surrounding 900 Rutledge Avenue is any less desirable than Petitioner’s
present neighborhood. To the contrary, the evidence indicates that the neighborhood is more
desirable, because it is an entirely residential area as opposed to a mixed residential and industrial
area; it is located away from major thoroughfares, as opposed to Petitioner’s present apartment; and
it has paved streets and sidewalks as opposed to the unpaved, dead end street on which Petitioner’s
present apartment is situated.
Moreover, the regulations do not require that a comparable replacement dwelling be in the
immediate vicinity of a displaced person’s employment. All that is required is that the comparable
replacement dwelling be “reasonably accessible” to the person’s place of employment. In this case,
the Petitioner presently lives on the Charleston peninsula and uses his own vehicle to travel to his
place of employment in Mt. Pleasant. Accordingly, I conclude that 900 Rutledge Avenue, which is
located several blocks away from Petitioner’s present apartment, is “reasonably accessible” to
Petitioner’s place of employment. See Respondent’s Exhibit 2.
Finally, regardless of the location of the comparable replacement dwelling used to compute
the rental assistance payment, a displaced person may move wherever he or she wishes to live and
may apply the rental assistance payment toward the cost of a new apartment. If the Petitioner wishes
to live in Mt. Pleasant, he is free to do so. However, the Department is not required to subsidize
Petitioner for the additional costs of living in Mt. Pleasant. The Department is only required to
compute the maximum rental assistance payment on the basis of a comparable replacement dwelling
in the same vicinity as Petitioner’s present apartment, as set forth in the regulations. I find and
7

conclude, based on the evidence presented, that the Department acted properly and within the
requirements of 49 C.F.R. Part 24 in computing a rental assistance payment for the Petitioner in the
amount of $10,500.00.
ORDER
Based upon the foregoing Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law, I find that the
Department’s decision to award the Petitioner Ten Thousand Five Hundred Dollars ($10,500) in
relocation assistance benefits was proper and is hereby affirmed.
AND IT IS SO ORDERED.
__________________________________
MARVIN F. KITTRELL
Chief Administrative Law Judge
August 14, 2001
Columbia, South Carolina
8

text:
STATE OF SOUTH CAROLINA
ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGE DIVISION
Civil Engineering Consulting Services, Inc., )

APPEARANCES: James Coffas, Esquire, for Petitioner
Linda C. McDonald, Esquire, for Respondent
STATEMENT OF THE CASE
This matter comes before the Administrative Law Judge Division ("Division") upon the
request of Petitioner Civil Engineering Consulting Services, Inc. (“CECS”) for a contested case
hearing pursuant to S.C. Code Ann. § 1-23-600(B) (Supp. 2001) and 25A S.C. Code Ann. Regs.
63-700 et seq. (Supp. 2001), challenging Respondent South Carolina Department of
Transportation’s ("Department"’s) denial of CECS's application for certification as a
Disadvantaged Business Enterprise ("DBE").
After notice to the parties, a final hearing before the Division was conducted on February
5, 2002. Upon review of the relevant and probative evidence and the applicable law, I find and
conclude that CECS's application for DBE certification should be denied.
FINDINGS OF FACT
After observing the witnesses and considering the testimony and evidence presented at
the hearing, I make the following Findings of Fact:
1. Notice of the date, time, place, and nature of the hearing was timely given to all
parties.
2. CECS is a consulting firm that offers expertise in highway planning and design,
project management, CADD application, environmental studies, value

engineering, expert witness testimony on transportation issues, quality
assurance/quality control, bridge design, construction engineering and inspection,
hydrological studies, and other fields related to transportation engineering.
3. Paul and Cathy Raad established CESC in 1993 with Cathy’s retirement funds
from her previous employment with Richland County School District One.
Although Cathy initially owned only 60% of CESC’s stock, in or around 1997,
Cathy bought out Paul’s interest. Today, Paul remains an employee of the firm
and is assigned to Fluor Daniel, where he has his own office.
4. Cathy Raad received a B.A. in education from the University of South Carolina in
1982. Prior to going into business with her husband, she taught in Richland
School District One from 1982-89. She ran an Import/Export Business for about
a year. Since the establishment of CECS in 1993, Cathy has worked full-time for
CECS as its president, putting in fifty-plus hours weekly. Cathy is responsible
for the day-to-day management of CECS.
5. Paul Raad received a B.S. in Civil Engineering from the University of Central
Florida in 1984 and an M.S. in Civil Engineering from the University of South
Carolina in 1987. He is a registered Professional Engineer in the States of South
Carolina, Florida, and Georgia, and the country of Lebanon. He worked for the
Department from 1985 to 1992, where he was in charge of over 100 engineers and
technicians in the Road Design Section and also a Project Engineer. He has
developed over 40 CADD Design/Highway design programs that analyze and
solve complex transportation problems. He has been the principal engineer for
CECS since 1993. During his employment with CECS, Paul has worked on the
following major transportation projects in the State, among others: Conway
Bypass, Southern Connector, Airport Access Road in Richland County, I-385
Widening, I-95/S-83 Interchange in Florence County; SC-101 Widening in
Spartanburg County, US 321 Widening in Orangeburg County; and
I-77/SC161/US21 Interchange Redesign in York County. Paul Raad has been
recognized as a “superstar” in the engineering field.
2

6. Paul is designated as CECS’s “Principal in Charge” for purposes of the Certificate
of Authorization issued by the South Carolina Department of Labor, Licensing
and Regulation’s Board of Professional Engineers and Land Surveyors.
7. In the year 2001, Paul was worked overseas in Lebanon or at Fluor Daniel’s
offices in Columbia, South Carolina, for a little over half of the year. He spent
39 days, or 10% of the time, overseas and 160 days, or 44% of the time, working
at Fluor Daniel’s offices. On both of these assignments he was working on
CECS business.
8. CECS employs eight professional engineers who are experienced in the areas of
environmental issues, hydraulics, bridge design, road design, and testifying.
These employees provide the technical expertise required by CECS’s clients.
Half of these engineers are non-disadvantaged individuals who were former
employees of the Department and were characterized as outstanding performers in
their fields: Paul Raad; H. L. Allen, a traffic and program engineer; Paul
Embler, who was the head of the Department’s environmental unit; and Russell
Howell, a project engineer and hydrology engineer.
9. Cathy is not a licensed professional engineer and is not competent to perform any
engineering work herself. Because she is not a licensed professional engineer,
she cannot sign off on engineering plans. Further, although Cathy does sign
proposals on behalf of the firm, she must receive help from one of the firm’s
engineers in preparing the proposals. Although she knows which engineers are
required to perform certain types of work, Cathy uses a form to see if CECS
has the personal and equipment to do a job. She confers with her engineers to
enable her to determine whether a job is going to be profitable. Cathy signs
contracts on behalf of the firm, makes financial decisions, management decisions
and policy-making decisions for the firm. On occasion, Cathy has worked out in
the field with other employees of the firm on certain projects. As President of
CECS, Cathy confers with the employees of her firm, including her husband,
about firm business.
3

10. Cathy has attended industry meetings and conferences where technical sessions
were offered.
11. James E. Scapellato, who testified on behalf of CECS, and his wife own a
consulting business; his wife owns 75% and he owns 25%. They provide
consulting service primarily in the area of safety and environment. They are also
looking into becoming certified as a DBE with the Department. Scapalleto is
familiar with CECS because the two firms provide similar services. Scapalleto
has seen Cathy in professional circles and they have attended the same meetings
and conferences at which technical matters were discussed. He finds her to be
knowledgeable and engaging in terms of the work that she does. Scapalleto has
observed her articulate and engage in meaningful discussions on
engineering-related subjects.
12. At the time of the hearing, the Department had certified thirty-nine firms that
provide consultative services, including engineering consultative services, as
DBE’s. At least two of those firms performing engineering consulting services
are owned by women.
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
Based upon the foregoing Findings of Fact, I conclude, as a matter of law, the following:
1. The Division has subject matter jurisdiction in this case pursuant to S.C. Code
Ann. § 1-23-600(B) (Supp. 2001) and 23A S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 63-704(K)
(Supp. 2001).
2. The Department is required to certify eligible firms to participate in the South
Carolina DBE program pursuant to S.C. Code Ann. § 12-28-2930(B) (Rev. 2000).
3. As a recipient of federal highway funds, the Department is also required to
implement a DBE program in compliance with 49 C.F.R. Part 26. The Department
has promulgated regulations to implement both the state and federal DBE
programs in South Carolina. See 25A S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 63-700 et seq. (Supp.
2001). Pursuant to the regulations, the Department has adopted the standards for
certifying DBEs, which are set forth in 49 C.F.R. Part 26. See 25A S.C. Code
4

Ann. Regs. 63-702(A) and 63-703(A) (Supp. 2001).
4. A DBE is defined generally as a small business concern owned and controlled by
a socially and economically disadvantaged individual. See 49 CFR, Subpart A,
Section 26.5. The regulations provide that woman owners are rebuttably
presumed to be socially and economically disadvantaged for purposes of the DBE
program. See 49 CFR Section 26.67(a). The regulations further set forth certain
rules to be used for determining whether or not the socially and economically
disadvantaged individual “owns” and “controls” the firm as required by the
eligibility standards. See 49 CFR 26.69 and 26.71.
5. A firm seeking certification as a DBE has the burden of demonstrating, by the
preponderance of the evidence, that it meets the requirements of 49 C.F.R. Part 26
concerning group membership or individual disadvantage, business size,
ownership, and control. 49 C.F.R. § 26.61. The Department does not contest
whether CECS meets the requirements of 49 CFR Part 26 as to group
membership, business size or ownership by a disadvantaged individual. The
Department contends only that the firm has failed to meet its burden of proving
that it meets the requirements for “control” by the woman-owner.
6. The DBE regulations require that:
The socially and economically disadvantaged owner must possess
the power to direct and cause the direction of the management and
policies of the firm and to make the day-to-day as well as
long-term decisions on matters of management, policy and
operations.
49 CFR Section 26.71(d).
7. In addition, the regulations provide the following in regard to the degree of
technical expertise required in order to control a firm within the meaning of the
DBE regulations:
the socially and economically disadvantaged owners must have an
overall understanding of, and managerial and technical competence
and experience directly related to, the type of business in which the
firm is engaged and the firm's operations. The socially and
5

economically disadvantaged owners are not required to have
experience or expertise in every critical area of the firm's
operations, or to have greater experience or expertise in a given
field than managers or key employees. The socially and
economically disadvantaged owners must have the ability to
intelligently and critically evaluate information presented by other
participants in the firm's activities and to use this information to
make independent decisions concerning the firm's daily operations,
management, and
policymaking. Generally, expertise limited to office management,
administration, or bookkeeping functions unrelated to the principal
business activities of the firm is insufficient to demonstrate control.
49 C.F.R. § 26.71(g).
The regulations require the disadvantaged owner to have “technical competence”
and experience directly related to the type of business in which the firm is
engaged and the firms operations. Unfortunately, however, the regulations do
not define “technical competence.”
8. At the very least, “technical competence” must consist of “a base level of
technical knowledge of the industry” and “a sufficient background and
expertise...with respect to delegated aspects of the business to be able to
intelligently use and critically evaluate information” presented by employees in
making “decisions concerning the daily operational activities of the business.”
See Car-Mar Construction Corp. v. Skinner, 777 F. Supp. 50, 55-56 (D.D.C.
1991).
9. In this case, CECS is an engineering consulting business whose primary product is
engineering expertise. Cathy does not possess engineering expertise gained from
either education or experience. She is not a professional, licensed engineer. She
cannot sign engineering plans, testify as an expert engineer, or perform
hydrological or environmental studies. Further, in response to the Department’s
line of questioning regarding her competence to perform a laundry list of basic
engineering functions, Cathy admitted she was not competent to perform them.
Given her admitted inability to perform such basic engineering tasks, it is difficult
6

to conceive that she could “critically evaluate” information presented by the
firm’s engineers and use that information to make independent decisions
on engineering matters in the daily operations of the firm. While this tribunal
acknowledges that Cathy can intelligently discuss the business of the firm and is
responsible for the majority of the firm’s marketing, such skills are primarily
managerial and administrative skills, and not the technical skills required by
regulations governing the certification of DBE’s.
10. This tribunal recognizes that in today’s world, the Chief Executive Officer of a
company often does not possess technical expertise in the area of business that he
or she manages. However, DBE regulations do not proscribe such a CEO from
owning and running a technical business. Rather, such regulations prescribe that
some minority owners are entitled to DBE certification so long as those minority
owners satisfy certain requirements. Therefore, I conclude that, although she
has managerial competence, Cathy Raad does not have the requisite technical
expertise to control the firm within the meaning of the DBE regulations.
ORDER
IT IS HEREBY ORDERED that CECS’s application for certification as a
Disadvantaged Business Enterprise is DENIED;
AND IT IS SO ORDERED.

ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGE
April 17, 2002
Columbia, South Carolina

materials

materials to the user of the materials. Customers call the Petitioner and request the pick up and
delivery.

King

the hearing that she owns 75% of the stock in the business. She stated she put 51% on the

Stenography/General Office. Since 1986 she has worked at Coastal Rapid Public Transit
Authority (CRPTA) in Conway, South Carolina. Over the course of the years she has held three
positions there, all of which involve administrative duties. The company is responsible for
transporting people to and from medical appointments. She is responsible for scheduling
seventeen drivers to transport Medicaid and elderly patients to medical appointments. Her
position with CRPTA is full-time.
5. JBK Trucking employs drivers to drive the trucks. The drivers are responsible for
picking up the materials and delivering them as instructed. Kathryn King does all of the
scheduling of JBK’s trucks. She negotiates the price with customers and instructs drivers on
where and when to pick up and deliver materials. At the time of the hearing the three trucks were
going to North Carolina twice a day to pick up rock.
6. John King has worked in the asphalt business for many years. For 22 years he
worked
for Palmetto Paving Corporation as the Asphalt Plant Manager. He left his employment at
Palmetto about the time JBK Trucking was being established. Temporarily it looked as though he
would resume work by driving a truck for JBK ; however, he accepted a job with Southern
Asphalt and has worked with them since 2000. He testified he stays extremely busy at Southern

King on a frequent basis because JBK transports materials for Southern Asphalt. It does not
appear that Mr. King sets up all of JBK’s business through his employment as the Respondent
alleges. The Petitioners submitted evidence of work they have done for other companies. There is

no doubt it is fortuitous for Mrs. King that her husband is now employed with a company that
uses JBK’s services, but I do not find that in any way puts Mr. King in control of JBK. The
Kings contend that the Department is wrong when it asserts John King is the one with

JBK;

DBE

father when he was still employed full-time as an officer with the South Carolina Highway
Patrol. He stated that he could not have run the company, which then had five trucks, while he

the power to direct and cause the direction of the management and
policies of the firm and to make the day-to-day as well as
4

long-term decisions on matters of management, policy and
operations.

technical expertise required in order to control a firm within the meaning of the
DBE regulations:

economically disadvantaged owners are not required to have

operations, or to have greater experience or expertise in a given
field than managers or key employees. The socially and
economically disadvantaged owners must have the ability to
intelligently and critically evaluate information presented by other
participants in the firm's activities and to use this information to
make independent decisions concerning the firm's daily operations,

policymaking. Generally, expertise limited to office management,
administration, or bookkeeping functions unrelated to the principal
business activities of the firm is insufficient to demonstrate control.
49 C.F.R. § 26.71(g).
The regulations require the disadvantaged owner to have “technical competence”
and
experience directly related to the type of business in which the firm is engaged and the firm’s
operations. Unfortunately, however, the regulations do not define “technical competence.”

technical
knowledge of the industry” and “a sufficient background and expertise...with respect to delegated
aspects of the business to be able to intelligently use and critically evaluate information”
presented by employees in making “decisions concerning the daily operational activities of the
business.” See Car-Mar Construction Corp. v. Skinner, 777 F. Supp. 50, 55-56 (D.D.C. 1991).
5

9. In this case, JBK Trucking is a hauling business whose primary product is
the transport of construction materials. Although Kathryn King does not possess expertise gained
from either education or experience in construction material or trucking maintenance, she does
possess the expertise in the field of transportation. While it is true that “office management,
administration, or bookkeeping functions unrelated to the principal business activities of the firm
is insufficient to demonstrate control”, here the coordination of the transportation is exactly the
business in which JBK Trucking is engaged.
10. The federal regulations address the issue of owners working in other jobs:
In order to be viewed as controlling a firm, a socially and
economically disadvantaged owner cannot engage in outside
employment or other business interests that conflict with the
management of the firm or prevent the individual from devoting
sufficient time an attention to the affairs of the firm to control its
activities. For example, absentee ownership of a business and
part-time work in a full-time firm are not viewed as constituting
control. However, an individual could be viewed as controlling a
part-time business that operates only on evenings and/or weekends,
if the individual controls it all the time it is operating.
49 C.F.R. §26.71 (j).
It is undisputed that Mrs. King works full-time for another employer. However, that

her from devoting sufficient time to JBK Trucking to control its activities. This seems obvious by

controlling the business.
ORDER
IT IS HEREBY ORDERED that the application for certification as a Disadvantaged
Business Enterprise of JBK Trucking, Inc. is GRANTED.
AND IT IS SO ORDERED.

APPEARANCES: Paul R. Rahn, Esquire, for Petitioner

STATEMENT OF THE CASE
This matter comes before the Administrative Law Judge Division (Division) upon the
request of Petitioner Strock Enterprises, Inc., for a contested case hearing pursuant to S.C. Code
Ann. §12-8-2930 (2000) and 25A S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 63-700 (Supp. 1999) et seq.concerning
the denial of Strock Enterprises, Inc.’s application for certification as a Disadvantaged Business
Enterprise (DBE).
After notice to the parties, a final hearing before the Division was conducted on July 31,
2002. Upon review of the relevant and probative evidence and the applicable law, I find that the
DBE Certification of Strock Enterprises, Inc. should be DENIED.
FINDINGS OF FACT
After observing the witnesses and considering the testimony and the evidence presented
at the hearing, I make the following Findings of Fact:
1. Notice of the date, time, place, and nature of the hearing was timely given to all
parties.
2. Strock Enterprises, Inc. is a construction firm engaged in the general commercial
and residential contracting and renovation business in Charleston and surrounding counties.
3. Stock Enterprises, Inc. was incorporated in October 1993, and Brenda Strock

became President of Strock Enterprises, Inc. She has held this position for the last nine years.
At the initial meeting of Strock Enterprises, Inc., Brenda Strock was issued 2616 shares of the
5000 outstanding shares of Strock Enterprises, Inc. stock.
4. Brenda Strock attended business college in Savannah, Georgia in 1965 and 1966,
where she studied accounting and business. She has worked in the accounting department at a
television station and in the construction field at Diamond Enterprises Construction of Savannah,
Georgia. She held this position for ten years before moving to Strock Enterprises, Inc. of
Georgia as an estimator and accountant. She coordinated with the subcontractors and did
layouts for the construction projects. She has over thirty years experience in the construction
business.
5. Regarding the South Carolina corporation at issue in this matter, Brenda Strock
works with the day to day administrative activities of Strock Enterprises, Inc. Her
responsibilities include management, financial decisions, estimating and accounting for Strock
Enterprises, Inc. She has the power to bind the corporation by entering into contracts on behalf
of the corporation. She signs all the corporate checks and has the authority to hire and fire
employees of the corporation. She manages the company, its finances and leases equipment on
behalf of the corporation. Her compensation from Strock Enterprises, Inc., as shown on the
corporate tax returns, was $22,945.00 in 1997, $24,854.00 in 1998 and $15,683.00 in 1999.
6. Thomas Strock, Brenda Strock’s husband, has worked as a carpenter since 1963.
He served an eight year apprenticeship in Savannah before working for Diamond Enterprises for
nine years. After that, he worked for Strock Enterprises in Georgia as a carpenter and estimator,
and has worked in a similar capacity for Strock Enterprises, Inc. of South Carolina since 1993.
Mr. Strock is the supervising contractor and estimator. He helps obtain jobs, purchase materials,
estimate bids and supervises the subcontractors and employees. He sat for the General
Contractor’s License Exam in 1999 on behalf of Strock Enterprises, Inc. He has extensive
experience in construction and contracting. His compensation from Strock Enterprises, Inc., as
shown on the corporate tax returns, was $28,341.00 in 1997, $44,219.00.00 in 1998 and
$27,572.00 in 1999.
7. Thomas “Trey” Strock, Brenda and Thomas’ son, is also now employed in the
family business and assists with overseeing the sub-contractors’ work on a day to day basis.

8. The construction process for Strock Enterprises, Inc. is as follows. Trey does the
sketches from the plans in order to give to the subcontractors for their bids. Trey and Thomas
Strock then assess the material and labor costs by checking books for the various materials
needed. Brenda Strock is able to do this aspect of the bid process, but Thomas and Trey do most
of it. Once the subcontractors have submitted their proposals, Strock Enterprises, Inc. makes
their presentation to the client. Although Brenda Strock has stated that she used to go out to
“wine and dine” the clients, Strock Enterprises, Inc. now receives the bulk of their business from
word of mouth. Trey Strock is shown as being in charge of “marketing and sales” for the
company. Once the client approves the bids, Brenda and Thomas set up a schedule for the
construction. They try to get contracts signed for the various aspects of work to be done, but a
good bit is done without a contract. Although Brenda formerly went to the job sites to assure
acceptable completion of the various aspects of work by the subcontractors, Thomas and Trey do
most of that now.
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
Based upon the foregoing Findings of Fact, I conclude, as a matter of law, the following:
1. The Division has subject matter jurisdiction in this case pursuant to S.C. Code
Ann.§ 1-23-600(B) (Supp. 2001) and 23A S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 63-704(K) (Supp. 2001).
2. The Department is required to certify eligible firms to participate in the South
Carolina DBE program pursuant to S.C. Code Ann. § 12-28-2930(B) (Rev. 2000). Businesses
receiving the certification are then allocated a certain percentage of highway funds for
construction and renovation projects.
3. As a recipient of federal highway funds, the Department is also required to
implement a DBE program in compliance with 49 CFR Part 26. The Department has
promulgated regulations to implement both the state and federal DBE programs in South
Carolina. See 25A S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 63-700 et seq. (Supp. 2001). Pursuant to the
regulations, the Department has adopted the standards for certifying DBEs, which are set forth in
49 CFR Part 26. See 25A S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 63-702(A) and 63-703(A) (Supp. 2001).
4. A DBE stands for Disadvantaged Business Enterprise and is defined generally as a
small business concern owned and controlled by a socially and economically disadvantaged
individual. See 49 CFR, Subpart A, Section 26.5. The regulations provide that woman owners

are rebuttably presumed to be socially and economically disadvantaged for purposes of the DBE
program. See 49 CFR Section 26.67(a). The regulations further set forth certain rules to be
used for determining whether or not the socially and economically disadvantaged individual
“owns” and “controls” the firm as required by the eligibility standards. See 49 CFR 26.69 and
26.71.
5. A business seeking certification as a DBE has the burden of demonstrating, by
the preponderance of the evidence, that it meets the requirements of 49 CFR Part 26 concerning
group membership or individual disadvantage, business size, ownership, and control. 49 CFR
Section 26.61. The Department contends only that the firm has failed to meet its burden of
proving that it meets the requirements for “ownership” and “control” by the woman-owner.
6. In this matter, although Brenda Strock owns 52% of the outstanding stock of
Strock Enterprises, Inc., which constitutes “ownership” of the company pursuant to 25 S.C.
Code Ann. Regs. 63-701 (N), the issue of the quality of that ownership must be addressed under
the Federal Regulations:
The firm’s ownership by socially and economically disadvantaged
individuals must be real, substantial, and continuing, going beyond pro
forma ownership of the firm as reflected in ownership documents. The
disadvantaged owners must enjoy the customary incidents of ownership,
and share in the risks and profits commensurate with their ownership
interests, as demonstrated by the substance, not merely the form , of
arrangements. 49 CFR, Section 26.69 (c) (Emphasis added.)
Here, Brenda Strock’s majority ownership is not borne out by her compensation which has been
significantly lower than that of her husband.
7. Furthermore the issue of control must also be addressed. In order to be classified
as a DBE, the second requirement of “control” must also be established by the applicant by a
preponderance of the evidence. The DBE regulations require that:
The socially and economically disadvantaged owner must possess the power to direct and cause
the direction of the management and policies of the firm and to make the day-to-day as well as
long-term decisions on matters of management, policy and operations.
49 CFR Section 26.71(d).
8. In addition, the regulations provide the following in regard to the degree of
technical expertise required in order to control a firm within the meaning of the DBE regulations:

The socially and economically disadvantaged owners must have an overall
understanding of, and managerial and technical competence and
experience directly related to, the type of business in which the firm is
engaged and the firm's operations. The socially and economically
disadvantaged owners are not required to have experience or expertise in
every critical area of the firm's operations, or to have greater experience or
expertise in a given field than managers or key employees. The socially
and economically disadvantaged owners must have the ability to
intelligently and critically evaluate information presented by other
participants in the firm's activities and to use this information to make
independent decisions concerning the firm's daily operations, management,
and policymaking. Generally, expertise limited to office management,
administration, or bookkeeping functions unrelated to the principal
business activities of the firm is insufficient to demonstrate control.
49 CFR Section 26.71(g), emphasis added.
The regulations require the disadvantaged owner to have “technical competence”
and experience directly related to the type of business in which the firm is engaged and the firm’s operations.
Unfortunately, however, the regulations do not define “technical competence.”
9. At the very least, “technical competence” must consist of “a base level of
technical knowledge of the industry” and “a sufficient background and expertise...with respect to
delegated aspects of the business to be able to intelligently use and critically evaluate
information” presented by employees in making “decisions concerning the daily operational
activities of the business.” See Car-Mar Construction Corp. v. Skinner, 777 F. Supp. 50, 55-56
(D.D.C. 1991).
10. The issue of family owned businesses is addressed in the Federal Regulations as
follows: “If you cannot determine that the socially and economically disadvantaged owners–as
distinct from the family as a whole–control the firm, then the socially and economically
disadvantaged owners have failed to carry their burden of proof concerning control, even though
they may participate significantly in the firm’s activities.” 49 CFR Section 26.71 (K)(2)
ORDER
Brenda Strock’s general background in finance, along with her extensive experience in
the field of construction finance and accounting, have been an asset to the company. It does not

appear, however, that the Petitioners have met their burden of proof to show either that Brenda
Strock “owns” or “controls” Strock Enterprises, Inc. as required by law. Her “ownership” is pro
forma and is not substantiated by the requisite indicia of ownership, including sharing in the

IT IS HEREBY ORDERED that the application for certification as a Disadvantaged
Business Enterprise of Strock Enterprises, Inc. is DENIED.
